content: Hepatitis D is a disease caused by the hepatitis delta virus (HDV), a small circular RNA virus. HDV is unique in that it cannot replicate independently and requires the presence of the hepatitis B virus (HBV) to propagate. Transmission of HDV can occur either through simultaneous infection with HBV (coinfection) or through infection of an individual already chronically infected with HBV (superinfection). Both coinfection and superinfection with HDV result in more severe complications compared to HBV infection alone. These complications include a higher risk of acute liver failure and an increased likelihood of developing chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma. Hepatitis D, when combined with HBV, has the highest mortality rate among all hepatitis infections, with a mortality rate of up to 20%. The hepatitis delta virus was first identified in 1977 by an Italian researcher, Mario Rizzetto. HDV infection is limited to the liver, as this is the only organ where the virus can replicate. The pathogenesis of HDV is not fully understood, but both the innate and adaptive immune systems are believed to play significant roles in the liver damage caused by the virus. Rarely, it may be transmitted perinatally. Different genotypes of HDV influence the virus's infectivity and disease progression. HDV belongs to the genus Deltavirus and has a single-stranded circular RNA genome with a high degree of complementarity, which allows it to survive under extreme conditions. The virus relies on the host cell for all stages of its life cycle, including attachment, penetration, uncoating, replication, assembly, and release. HDV also depends on HBV to provide the protein components necessary for its envelope. The virus is composed of several particles, including HBsAg, HDAg-S, HDAg-L, and RNA. Humans are the natural reservoir for HDV, and the virus specifically targets hepatocytes. Hepatitis D must be differentiated from other conditions that cause similar symptoms, such as fever, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and elevated liver enzymes. These conditions include other forms of viral hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis. HDV infection affects over 15 million people worldwide, primarily in regions such as Central Africa, the Mediterranean Basin, the Amazon Basin, and parts of Asia. However, the prevalence of HDV is decreasing in many areas due to HBV vaccination programs, improved education, and better socioeconomic conditions. Screening for HDV is recommended for individuals who are HBsAg-positive, those with acute or chronic hepatitis, and individuals who are IgM anti-HBc positive but HBsAg-negative. Blood products should also be screened to prevent transmission through transfusions or hemodialysis. HDV infection progresses through four phases: the incubation period, the preicteric phase, the icteric phase, and the convalescence phase. Coinfection with HBV and HDV often results in acute hepatitis, with most patients clearing the infection. However, superinfection in individuals with chronic HBV infection frequently leads to fulminant hepatitis, chronic active hepatitis, cirrhosis, and liver failure. Chronic HDV infection is associated with a higher risk of complications, including hepatocellular carcinoma. Symptoms of HDV infection include fever, jaundice, fatigue, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dark urine, and loss of appetite. Physical examination findings may include jaundice, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites, and signs of portal hypertension in advanced disease. The diagnosis of HDV is confirmed by detecting HDV RNA in the blood using RT-PCR. Serologic markers such as HDAg and anti-HD antibodies (IgM and IgG) may also be used. Liver biopsy may be performed to assess the stage of liver disease, and imaging studies such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound can help monitor complications like cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Genotyping of HDV can provide insights into disease severity and treatment response. Currently, there is no effective antiviral therapy for HDV. Pegylated interferon-α is the only drug with demonstrated antiviral activity against HDV, but its efficacy is limited, and most patients remain HDV RNA-positive after treatment. Long-term treatment with nucleos(t)ide analogs (NUCs) may reduce HBsAg levels in some patients. Chronic HDV infection is typically treated with weekly injections of pegylated interferon for at least 48 weeks. Liver transplantation may be necessary for patients with end-stage liver disease, liver failure, or hepatocellular carcinoma secondary to HDV infection. Prevention of HDV infection relies on vaccination against HBV, as HDV cannot infect individuals who are not already infected with HBV. Research into new therapies for HDV is ongoing, with potential treatments targeting viral assembly, post-translational modifications, and HBV entry. Investigational drugs, such as prenylation inhibitors and novel forms of interferons, are being studied for their efficacy and tolerability in treating HDV.
